newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Westin Hotels sees strong growth in Asia-Pacific.
newsitem.headline: Westin Hotels sees strong growth in Asia-Pacific.

text.p: Westin Hotels & Resorts plans to double the number of hotels and resorts in the Asia-Pacific region over the next few years, regional president Theodore Teng said on Thursday.

"Asia is such a dynamic part of the world, we are going to set our target to be half of the company's overall goal, that is one every other month or six hotels a year," Teng told a news conference after a meeting of Asia-Pacific general managers.
This would increase the number of managed and franchise hotels in the region to 35 by the year 2000.
In 1995, the company set out to acquire one new hotel per month for the next five years.
Teng said Westin's operating philosophy was to set aggressive goals and to implement a plan to exceed it.
"I have a very strong feeling we will sign about eight (new hotels) this year," he said.
The areas targetted for growth were China, Hong Kong, India, Australia and New Zealand.
The group runs 19 hotels and resorts in the Asia-Pacific region and its newest property in the region, The Westin Resort in Guam, in February.
Other hotels under development are in Kuala Lumpur, set to begin next year, and Jakarta, in 1999.
Westin operates more than 100 hotels and resorts in 23 countries, and recent growth was largely in the United States.
Asked about future growth trends, Curt Ewald, vice president of sales and marketing in the Asia-Pacific, said U.S. expansion was slowing.
"Older hotels in the U.S. are re-flagged under our management but in Asia, hotels tend to be new," Ewald said.
He said it was easier to acquire hotels in the United States, owned mostly by institutions which seek Westin's managerial expertise.
In Asia, however, hotels are usually owned by corporations or are family-run and owners prefer to retain management control, he said.
Westin's expansion in Asia will see a shift to more resort hotels and larger rooms for families.
"We are looking at the travelling patterns of the region rather than adopting the cookie-cutter approach, as in North America," Teng said.
"As the income level of Asia grows, there will be a huge demand for resorts," Teng said.
He said many Asians travelled with families, or as groups of couples with children. Westin would re-configure rooms to include common corridors and common areas.

Teng said he would not speculate on any future change in ownership. The Wall Street Journal's electronic edition said last month said Westin Hotels & Resorts could be sold for as much as S1 billion or more.
Westin said in November it or an affiliate was considering an initial public offering of common stock this year.
Proceeds from the offering would be used for general corporate purposes, including the repayment of loans.
--Jacqueline Wong, Singapore newsroom (65 8703080)
